code.title: JSX compiles to plain element objects

followUps:
A Fragment is an invisible wrapper that lets a component return several siblings without adding an extra DOM element. You need one because a component can return only one root. Write <><h1/><p/></> for the short form.

Use the long form <Fragment key={id}> when you map over a list and each item produces several elements, since the short form cannot take a key. Fragments matter for valid HTML too: a <tr> cannot sit inside an extra <div>, so a wrapper element would break a table.

It protects against injected fake elements, a kind of XSS. Every real element created by React carries $$typeof: Symbol.for('react.element') (a Symbol in current versions). JSON from a server cannot contain a Symbol, because JSON has no Symbol type.

So if an attacker stores something like {"type":"div","props":{...}} in the database and your code renders that JSON as a child, React checks $$typeof, sees it is missing, and refuses to treat it as an element. Without the check, user-controlled data could pose as markup.

Yes, JSX is only sugar. <div className="x">Hi</div> is the same as the plain call below, and the result is identical.

import { createElement as h } from 'react';
h('div', { className: 'x' }, 'Hi');
// with a child component:
h(Card, { name: 'Asha' }, h('p', null, 'Hello'));

Nobody writes it this way for large UIs because nested calls are hard to read. Some small projects use it to avoid a build step, often via a helper such as htm, which gives a template-string syntax that runs straight in the browser.

It can, but copying a prop into state is usually a bug because the state ignores later prop changes. useState(props.price) uses the prop only on the first render. If the parent later sends 20 instead of 10, your component still shows 10, so the parent and child disagree.

Copying is fine when the prop is only an initial value and you say so in the name, such as initialPrice. Otherwise read the prop directly, or reset the child with key={id} so it remounts with fresh state when the identity changes.

The child calls a function that the parent passed down as a prop. Data flows down as props, and events flow up as callbacks.

function Parent() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  return <Child onAdd={() => setN(n + 1)} />;
}
function Child({ onAdd }) { return <button onClick={onAdd}>+1</button>; }

The click runs the parent's function, the parent's state changes, and the parent re-renders. For distant components use Context or a store instead of passing callbacks through many levels.

Rarely, and usually only as a deliberate choice. Derived state means a value computed from other values, such as fullName from first and last. Normally compute it in render each time: it is cheap and cannot go stale.

You store it only when it must not follow the source automatically. Examples: a draft form initialised from a saved record and then edited freely by the user, or an expensive result you keep with useMemo (memoised, not stored in state). If you store it, name it clearly and decide when it resets, for example with a key.

code.title: Index key vs id key after deleting a row

followUps:
Delete the first item of a list whose rows hold typed text, using index as the key. Take rows Ann, Bob, Cy where you typed a note in Ann's input. After deleting Ann, the keys are now 0 (Bob) and 1 (Cy). Key 0 existed before, so React reuses Ann's old input and its state for Bob. The note "note for Ann" now appears in Bob's row.

The program above shows exactly this. With key={item.id} the note leaves with Ann, as it should.

No. key (like ref in older React) is consumed by React itself and is not passed to the component in props. Reading props.key gives undefined, and React warns about it in development.

If the child needs the same value, pass it a second time under another name: <Row key={item.id} id={item.id} />. Also, the key only needs to be unique among siblings in the same array, not across the whole page.

Change the key and React treats it as a different component, so the old one unmounts and a fresh one mounts with new state. This is the clean way to reset a component without writing reset code.

<ProfileForm key={user.id} user={user} />

When the selected user.id changes from 7 to 8, the form is rebuilt with empty fields and fresh effects. The cost is a full remount of that subtree, so do it only where a reset is really wanted.

It happens when value starts as undefined (React treats the input as uncontrolled) and later becomes a real value (now controlled). Example: useState() with no argument, then the user types, so the state goes from undefined to "a".

Fix it by always giving a defined value: useState(''), or value={form.name ?? ''} when data loads from an API. Choose one mode for the lifetime of the input. Never switch between value and defaultValue.

A file input is always uncontrolled, because browsers do not let code set a file path for security reasons. You cannot use value on it. Read the files when needed, from an onChange event or a ref.

<input type="file" onChange={e => {
  const file = e.target.files[0];
  setFile(file); // keep the File object in state
}} />

The File object is what you keep in state. To clear the input after upload, reset the form or change the input's key.

Stop storing every field in one parent's state, so a keystroke re-renders only one field. Three common options:

  • Uncontrolled inputs read on submit (FormData) or React Hook Form, which subscribes only to fields that need it.
  • Field components that own their value and report to the parent on blur.
  • Memoised field components with stable callbacks.

Example: 100 fields each re-rendering per key press is 100 renders; with local state it is 1.

code.title: State snapshot and the update queue

followUps:
Nothing visible happens: React compares the new value with the old using Object.is and, if they are equal, skips the re-render and does not update children or effects. React may still call the component function once more before it bails out, but the output and effects do not run again.

This is why setCount(5) when count is already 5 is cheap. It is also why setting an object or array to a mutated version of itself does nothing, as the reference is the same.

Yes. Since React 18, automatic batching applies to all updates, including those inside setTimeout, promises and native event handlers. Before 18, only updates inside React event handlers were batched, so each setState in a timeout caused its own render.

Example: after await fetch(...) you call setLoading(false) and setData(d). In React 18 that makes one render, not two. This needs the createRoot API.

flushSync forces React to apply the updates inside its callback to the DOM immediately and synchronously, instead of batching them for later.

flushSync(() => setItems(next));
listRef.current.scrollTop = listRef.current.scrollHeight;

The line after it sees the updated DOM. Use it rarely, for example to measure or scroll right after an update. It costs performance because it blocks batching, and it cannot be called during render.

Memo compares props with Object.is one by one, and anything that is a new object, array or function on each parent render counts as changed. Example: <Row style={{ a: 1 }} onClick={() => go(id)} /> creates a new object and a new function every render, so memo(Row) never skips.

Fix by hoisting constants outside the component, wrapping callbacks in useCallback and objects in useMemo, or relying on the React Compiler. Also children passed as JSX are new elements each time, which defeats memo.

It lets a wrapper component re-render without re-rendering the expensive part, because the expensive element was created by a parent that did not re-render. When the wrapper's state changes, props.children is the same element reference as before, so React skips it.

function Mouse({ children }) {
  const [pos, setPos] = useState(0); // changes often
  return <div onMouseMove={e => setPos(e.x)}>{children}</div>;
}
<Mouse><HeavyChart /></Mouse>

HeavyChart does not re-render on every mouse move.

The React Compiler is a build-time tool that analyses your components and automatically adds the memoisation you would write by hand with memo, useMemo and useCallback. It works only if your code follows the rules of React: pure render, no mutation of props or state.

The benefit is that most manual memoisation becomes unnecessary and code stays simpler. It does not fix structural problems such as state placed too high, so you still measure with the Profiler.

Put state in the closest common parent of everything that reads or changes it, and no higher. Ask: who displays it, who edits it? Find the lowest component that contains them all.

Example: a search box and a results list both need query, so their parent owns it. A tooltip's open/closed flag only matters to the tooltip, so it stays inside it. If data comes from a server and is shared across pages, a cache library such as TanStack Query can own it instead of a component.

Lifting too high makes more components re-render on every change and forces you to pass props through components that do not care. State in the app root means typing in one input re-renders the whole page.

It also hurts reuse and readability: a small widget now depends on its ancestors for data and callbacks. Example: lifting a modal's open flag to the root means a button three levels deep needs onOpen passed through every layer. Keep state close, and lift only when a second component needs it.

Context is a way to avoid passing lifted state through many levels. The state still lives in a parent (the provider), but any descendant can read it with useContext without props in between.

The trade-off: every consumer re-renders when the context value changes, so keep contexts small and focused (a theme context, not one giant app context). For rarely changing values like theme or the current user it fits well; for fast-changing values consider splitting or an external store.

Pick a render prop when the caller must decide what to draw from the data, and a custom hook when the caller only needs the logic. A hook shares behaviour (useMouse() returns x and y) with no extra nesting. A render prop gives the child a function to put output in a specific place: <List items={xs} renderItem={x => <Row x={x} />} />.

Today hooks replace most render props. Render props remain useful for list components, virtualisers and components that own the layout but not the content.

A compound component is a group of components that work together and share hidden state, like HTML's <select> and <option>. The parent owns the state and shares it through Context; the children read it.

<Tabs defaultValue="a">
  <Tabs.List><Tabs.Tab id="a">One</Tabs.Tab></Tabs.List>
  <Tabs.Panel id="a">Hello</Tabs.Panel>
</Tabs>

The caller controls order and markup, with no long list of props.

Elements passed in as children or other props are created by the parent, so when the wrapper's own state changes, those elements keep the same reference and React skips re-rendering them. This is the "children as props" trick.

Example: a collapsible panel that opens and closes re-renders only its frame, while a 1,000-row table passed as children is not rendered again. It gets the benefit of memo without writing memo.

code.title: Why mutating state skips re-render

followUps:
Memo compares references one level deep. If you copy the outer array but mutate an inner object, the outer reference changes (so the parent re-renders), but the row's item prop is still the same object as before.

const next = [...items];
next[1].done = true;      // same object
setItems(next);           // memo(Row) sees item === old item: skips

The data changed, but the row skips rendering, so the screen shows the old checkbox. The fix is items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, done: true } : i), which gives the changed item a new reference.

Immer gives you a temporary draft object (a Proxy) that records your changes, then produces a new immutable object that copies only what changed and shares the rest.

const next = produce(state, draft => {
  draft.todos[0].done = true;
});
// state is untouched; next has a new todos array and todo 0

Untouched branches keep their old references, so memo still works for them. It saves you from deep spread code like { ...s, todos: [...] }. In React you often use it through useImmer or Redux Toolkit.

Yes. Mutating a variable you create inside the render function is fine, because no one else can see it. Example: const out = []; for (...) out.push(...); return out is normal. It is called local mutation.

What is not allowed is mutating anything that existed before the render: props, state, context values or module variables. Render must be pure, so the same inputs give the same output, which is also why Strict Mode renders twice to expose such bugs.

The render phase works out what the UI should look like, and the commit phase actually changes the screen. Render calls your components and diffs the result, and it must be pure because React may pause, repeat or throw it away. Commit touches the real DOM, in one uninterruptible step.

Why it matters: side effects such as network calls or subscriptions must not run during render. They belong in event handlers or useEffect, which run after commit. Example: a console.log in render may print twice in Strict Mode; a log in an effect prints once per commit.

A fiber is React's internal object for one unit of work: one per component or DOM node in the tree. It stores the type, props, state (the hooks list), pointers to parent, first child and sibling, and the pending update queue.

Because fibers are linked in a list-like structure and not recursive calls, React can stop after any fiber, handle something urgent, and resume later. React keeps two trees (current and work-in-progress) and swaps them at commit.

In concurrent rendering, React can interrupt a render, work on something more urgent, and come back, instead of finishing in one block. Updates have priorities: typing is urgent, a big list filter can be marked as a transition with startTransition.

Example: while the user types, React shows the input update immediately and renders the heavy results in the background, dropping stale work if more typing arrives. Because render may run several times or be abandoned, it must stay pure. The commit phase is still synchronous.

code.title: count && Badge renders 0

followUps:
Strings render as text, including an empty string (which shows nothing visible, but still exists as a node). Numbers render, including 0 and NaN. false, true, null and undefined render nothing. An empty array renders nothing too.

Objects that are not elements (like a plain {a: 1} or a Date) throw an error: "Objects are not valid as a React child". Convert them first, for example date.toISOString(). Functions are ignored with a warning.

Use one status value instead of several booleans. Separate booleans like isLoading, isError and data can disagree (loading and error true together). A single state cannot.

const [state, setState] = useState({ status: 'loading' });
// { status: 'error', error } | { status: 'success', data }
if (state.status === 'loading') return <Spinner />;
if (state.status === 'error') return <Err e={state.error} />;

Libraries like TanStack Query already give you this shape.

Whether a component is rendered decides if its state lives or dies. When a condition turns false, the component unmounts and its state is lost; when it turns true again, it starts fresh.

Example: {open && <Editor />} loses the typed text each time you close it, while hiding with CSS (display: none) keeps it. Two branches of the same type at the same position, such as a ternary with two <Input />, share state. Use a different key to separate them.

Use real controls and the standard ARIA pattern. Each header is a <button> (focusable, Enter and Space work for free) with aria-expanded and aria-controls pointing to the panel's id. The panel has role="region" and aria-labelledby.

Add arrow-key handling: Down and Up move focus between headers (wrap around), Home and End jump to the first and last. Use a roving tabindex or let Tab move through headers normally. Hidden panels use hidden so screen readers skip them.

Support both by letting the parent supply value or fall back to internal state. If value is not undefined, you are controlled and call onValueChange; otherwise you keep your own state starting from defaultValue.

const isControlled = value !== undefined;
const [inner, setInner] = useState(defaultValue);
const current = isControlled ? value : inner;
function change(v) { if (!isControlled) setInner(v); onValueChange?.(v); }

Do not switch modes during the component's life.

Split the interactive part from the static part. The accordion needs state and click handlers, so the container is a Client Component ('use client'). The content inside can still be Server Components, passed as children, because the client component does not import them, it only receives their rendered output.

Example: a server-rendered FAQ answer with database text is placed inside a client <Accordion.Panel>. The compound API with Context also works, since Context needs client components.

code.title: When state is kept or reset

followUps:
Change the key to the user id: <UserForm key={user.id} user={user} />. When the selected user changes from 7 to 8, React unmounts the old form and mounts a new one with fresh state from the new user's data.

The alternative is to write effect code that copies new props into state, which is more code and flickers with stale values for one render. Key reset is simpler and has no stale frame. Remember it also resets child state, such as scroll positions inside.

Defining a component inside another creates a brand-new function each render. React compares types by reference, sees a different type, and unmounts the old subtree and mounts a new one. A new input element replaces the old one, so focus and state are lost.

function Form() {
  function Field() { return <input />; } // new type every render
  return <Field />;
}

Move Field outside Form and pass what it needs as props.

Rendering decides identity: a component that is not rendered has no instance, so no state. Putting the same type at the same position in both branches keeps state, putting different types resets it.

Example: {admin ? <Panel role="a" /> : <Panel role="b" />} keeps one Panel and its state, while {admin ? <Panel /> : <p>No</p>} destroys it. To keep state while hiding, render it and hide with CSS, or lift the state up to a parent that stays mounted.

You get speed, but give up some convenience. Uncontrolled inputs keep their value in the DOM, so React does not re-render per keystroke. The trade-offs: live features such as instant validation, formatting while typing, or showing a value elsewhere on the page need extra wiring (watchers, refs, events).

Setting values from code (reset, prefill) goes through a library API or a ref and not a simple state update. A common middle path is React Hook Form: uncontrolled by default, with Controller for the few fields that must be controlled.

Share one rule definition, such as a schema, and run it in both places. Libraries like Zod or Yup let you write z.object({ email: z.string().email() }) once in a shared module and import it in the browser and the server.

The client uses it for quick feedback; the server must still validate everything, because a client can be bypassed. Return field errors in a fixed shape such as { field: message } so the form can show them. Rules that need the database (is this email taken?) stay server-only.

Look at which components are wide and bright, meaning they rendered and took time. Turn on "Record why each component rendered" and check the reason: state changed, parent rendered, or props changed.

In the form case you would see 200 fields highlighted on every keystroke with the reason "parent rendered". That tells you to move state down or memoise. Also look for one very wide bar (an expensive child) and for components that render when nothing visible changed.

State is stored by React in the instance, in the fiber for that component, not in your function. The function runs again on every render and its local variables are lost, while hooks look up the saved values by call order.

That is why hooks must be called in the same order each time: the second useState call reads the second slot. It is also why state is lost when the instance unmounts, and why two copies of the same component each have their own state.

React compares the new element tree with the previous one, node by node. First it compares type: if it differs, the old subtree is removed and a new one built. If the type is the same, it keeps the instance and compares props, updating only what changed. For lists it uses key to match children.

Example: <div class="a"> to <div class="b"> only changes the class attribute; <div> to <span> rebuilds the subtree.

Elements are frozen in development (Object.freeze) because React relies on them being snapshots of one render. Diffing compares the previous element with the new one; if you mutated an element after creating it, the old and new would be the same object and React could not tell what changed.

Immutability also makes elements safe to reuse: the same element can be returned again, as with props.children, and React can skip work when it sees the same reference. To change the UI, create a new element.
